summary:
A tiny chemical feature may help explain why RNA can gather into droplets before a cell membrane surrounds it. Researchers led by the University at Buffalo compared RNA with single-stranded DNA and found that changing one chemical group strongly affected how the molecules assembled.

The study was published in Nature Communications on July 31, 2026. The university reported it on August 19, and ScienceDaily featured it on October 1. These are different reporting dates for the same research, rather than three separate discoveries.

The question matters to the RNA world hypothesis, which proposes that RNA played an important role in the emergence of life. RNA can store genetic information and help chemical reactions happen. Yet researchers still need to explain how fragile RNA molecules could gather and interact before cells provided enclosed spaces.

Liquid-like droplets called condensates offer one possible answer. They concentrate molecules without a membrane. In the laboratory comparison, RNA began forming droplets at temperatures about ten degrees Celsius lower than corresponding single-stranded DNA with similar sequences. RNA also more readily formed connected networks within droplets, helping the material shift toward a gel-like state.

The team investigated a chemical group called 2′-OH on RNA's sugar. DNA's sugar lacks this group. Using temperature-controlled microscopy, X-ray scattering and molecular dynamics simulations, the researchers explored how this structural difference changed interactions between molecules.

Their results suggest that the group strengthens RNA's interactions with magnesium ions. RNA also has fewer water molecules surrounding its backbone than DNA. Together, these properties make it easier for RNA molecules to approach one another as temperature rises. Chemically modifying the group reduced the tendency to form condensates and changed their material behavior.

The result links molecular chemistry to larger structures, but it does not demonstrate that these particular droplets produced the first living cells. Possible protection of early RNA remains an interpretation about the past, rather than direct observation. The team is now working toward RNA compartments that perform basic biochemical activities. Whether such systems can reproduce more features of cells is a question for further experiments.
title: RNA Droplets Reveal the Power of One Chemical Group
why_it_matters: The study connects small chemical differences with the formation of larger molecular compartments.
